text: In an age when anyone can disseminate information within seconds, distinguishing credible journalism from misleading content has become a matter of genuine discernment. Some outlets, driven by competition for attention, sensationalize stories or even fabricate details outright, sacrificing objectivity for clicks. Such practices not only undermine public trust but also skew our collective understanding of events. Readers, meanwhile, often retreat into an echo chamber, consuming only content that confirms existing beliefs, which leaves them increasingly gullible to misinformation. Were journalists held more rigorously accountable, notwithstanding the commercial pressures they face, standards of integrity might improve considerably. Reputable publications, to their credit, issue a retraction when errors come to light, subjecting their own work to the same scrutiny they apply to others. Nevertheless, verifying every claim before publication remains a daunting task in a fast-moving news cycle. Consequently, media literacy has never mattered more: citizens must learn to question sources, cross-check facts, and recognize when discourse has been deliberately skewed. Only then can the public discredit genuinely false narratives, rather than dismissing inconvenient truths as mere bias.
